implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the latch as sync.WaitGroup: Add(n) before the goroutines start, Done() on every exit path, Wait() in the collector; goroutines that can fail use golang.org/x/sync/errgroup, whose Wait() adds first-error propagation and, with WithContext, cancels the siblings. What the standard library does not ship is a reusable phase barrier - that is the channel or sync.Cond variant below. Respect the reuse rules: a WaitGroup must not be copied after first use and must not be re-armed with Add while a Wait is in flight; use one WaitGroup per round.
pitfalls: WaitGroup reuse race: calling Add on a WaitGroup while another goroutine is inside Wait panics or races; each round needs its own WaitGroup or the barrier variant.
The loop-variable capture bug (pre-Go 1.22): `go func(){...}()` closing over the loop variable makes every worker process the last element, and the WaitGroup happily waits for the duplicated work.

Wrong move: let a worker panic without a deferred Done or error path -> failure: without deferred Done a WaitGroup waiter can block, and an unrecovered panic terminates the process even if Done runs -> instead: defer Done immediately and recover or return the error through errgroup so the group can cancel.
Copying a WaitGroup into a helper by value is a data race the race detector flags; pass a pointer or keep it in the enclosing scope.

variants.name: Channel-based reusable phase barrier
variants.idiom_name: arrival channel + per-generation release gates, or sync.Cond with a generation counter
variants.implementation_notes: Because the standard library has no barrier type, Go composes one: each worker sends its arrival on a shared channel, a gatekeeper goroutine consumes all n arrivals and then closes the release gate for that generation, and workers block on `<-gate`. Closing instead of sending makes the release a broadcast, gives every later reader an immediate zero-value, and keeps the generation explicit; a sync.Cond with a generation counter is the other idiomatic composition, cheaper in allocations but without select-based cancellation. Prefer channels when cancellation matters (select on ctx.Done()) and Cond when the barrier is on a hot path with a fixed party count.
pitfalls: A gatekeeper goroutine leaks if a worker never arrives: give the barrier a context-aware select (`select { case arrived <- struct{}{}: case <-ctx.Done(): }`) so cancellation releases the group.
Closing a channel the next generation also uses panics on a second close; allocate one gate per generation up front (or hand the new gate through a channel) instead of reusing the same channel.

The release is a memory barrier only for data that happens-before the close: publishing partial results through a shared slice without an explicit synchronization (channel or mutex) races, because closing a channel does not make unrelated writes visible by accident.
